Councils levels 1-3 of 19 (new chronological reorg, per CURRICULUM-PLAN.md): what makes a council ecumenical (largely new, plus old live level 1's own definitional content), then Nicaea I (325) and Constantinople I/Ephesus (381, 431) each given a dedicated level, reusing old live level 1's council-specific content. CCC 465/466/884/195, council citations for Nicaea/Ephesus/Constantinople I already reviewed, and Acts 15:1-29 (reviewed in Church History) are reused here; other Scripture references are new and flagged by onramp_tool.py check.

questions.prompt: What makes a council 'ecumenical' rather than local or regional?
choices: It gathers the bishops of the whole Church in union with the Pope, and its teaching binds the universal Church
It is attended by more than three hundred bishops drawn from many different regions
It is held specifically in a city that itself has an apostolic see going back to the apostles
It formally lasts longer than a single full calendar year from start to finish
questions.correctAnswer: It gathers the bishops of the whole Church in union with the Pope, and its teaching binds the universal Church
questions.explanation: The criterion is universality and union with the Pope, not size or setting. Many large and important synods were never ecumenical, because the college of bishops does not act as a college apart from its head.
questions.hint: The test is about who is gathered and with whom, not how many or where.

questions.prompt: True or False: The Council of Jerusalem, described in Acts 15, is traditionally seen as an early pattern for how later councils would resolve disputed questions for the whole Church.
questions.explanation: True. The apostles gathered, deliberated, and issued a decision binding on the whole Church -- a small-scale preview of every ecumenical council that would follow across the next two thousand years, the whole subject of this topic.
questions.hint: Recall the very first council-like gathering, described early in the Acts of the Apostles.

questions.prompt: What kind of question does an ecumenical council typically gather to resolve?
choices: A serious dispute over faith, morals, or Church order that affects the whole Church, not just one region
A purely local administrative matter, like a single diocese's property dispute
A question that has never before been discussed anywhere in the Church
A matter already fully and finally settled, requiring no real deliberation at all
questions.correctAnswer: A serious dispute over faith, morals, or Church order that affects the whole Church, not just one region
questions.explanation: Councils are not called for routine business -- across this topic's whole chronological arc, every ecumenical council responds to a real, serious question the wider Church needs resolved together.
questions.hint: Consider the scale of the questions serious enough to require gathering bishops from across the whole Church.

questions.prompt: True or False: An ecumenical council's teaching requires papal confirmation to bind the whole Church.
questions.explanation: True, and this connects directly to level 1's own definition -- a council is ecumenical precisely because the bishops act in union with the Pope, not as an independent body apart from him.
questions.hint: Recall this level's own definition of what makes a council ecumenical in the first place.

questions.prompt: The Church has recognized twenty-one ecumenical ____ across its whole history, from the fourth century to the twentieth.
questions.explanation: This number -- twenty-one, not an open-ended or uncertain count -- is itself worth holding onto: this topic's whole chronological journey will trace every single one of them in order.
questions.hint: The word this whole topic is named for.

questions.prompt: Match each term to what it means for understanding this whole topic.

pairs.right: Representing the whole Church, in union with the Pope
An early apostolic-era pattern for later councils
What makes a council's teaching bind the whole Church
The total number of ecumenical councils this topic will cover

questions.explanation: These four pieces together define exactly what this topic is about, and set the scale of the journey ahead -- twenty-one real, distinct gatherings, not a vague or open-ended category.
questions.hint: Two rows define the term itself; two set up the scope of what follows.

questions.prompt: Does the size of a gathering of bishops, by itself, determine whether a council is ecumenical?
choices: No -- union with the Pope and universal scope are what matter, not headcount alone
Yes -- any gathering of at least one hundred bishops counts as ecumenical
Yes -- ecumenical status depends entirely on attendance numbers
No -- ecumenical status depends only on how long the gathering lasted
questions.correctAnswer: No -- union with the Pope and universal scope are what matter, not headcount alone
questions.explanation: A large regional synod is still not ecumenical if it lacks that union and universal scope; a smaller gathering meeting the real criteria is. Size is a common but mistaken shortcut for the actual test.
questions.hint: Recall this level's own stated criterion for ecumenical status.

questions.prompt: True or False: Every ecumenical council in this topic's whole chronological arc was called to resolve a question the wider Church genuinely needed settled.
questions.explanation: True. From Nicaea's confrontation with Arianism, the very next level in this topic, all the way through the twentieth century, no council in this topic was convened for a trivial or merely ceremonial reason.
questions.hint: Consider whether any council in Church history was ever called for a purely ceremonial reason.

questions.prompt: Given this level's definition of an ecumenical council, what does the next level in this topic turn to?
choices: The very first ecumenical council itself -- Nicaea, in 325
A complete repeat of this same level's definitional material
A jump directly to the Second Vatican Council in the 20th century
A subject entirely unrelated to councils or to the Church's own teaching authority
questions.correctAnswer: The very first ecumenical council itself -- Nicaea, in 325
questions.explanation: Having defined the category, this topic now moves in strict chronological order -- the next level meets the very first council to meet the definition this level has just established.
questions.hint: This is exactly what the next level in this topic covers.

questions.prompt: The Church's very first council-like gathering, described in Acts 15, met in the city of ____ to settle whether Gentile converts needed circumcision.
questions.explanation: This apostolic-era gathering, long before the word 'ecumenical' was ever applied to a council, already shows the same basic pattern this whole topic traces: bishops (here, the apostles themselves) gathering to settle a real question for the whole Church.
questions.hint: The same city this gathering, described in Acts 15, takes its name from.

questions.prompt: Which ecumenical council, held in 325, condemned Arius and produced the first part of what we now call the Nicene Creed?
choices: Nicaea
Ephesus
Chalcedon
Trent
questions.explanation: The First Council of Nicaea (325) confessed that the Son is 'of the same substance' as the Father and condemned Arius's teaching that the Son was a creature.
questions.hint: The city's name is the first word of the Creed said at Mass every Sunday.

citations.quote: God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father.
The Son of God is 'begotten, not made, of the same substance (homoousios) as the Father.'

questions.prompt: True or False: The First Council of Nicaea (325) is traditionally said to have been attended by around 318 bishops.
questions.explanation: Tradition remembers Nicaea as gathering roughly 318 bishops from across the Church, though exact ancient headcounts are naturally imprecise.
questions.hint: Tradition remembers a very specific, often-repeated number for this gathering.

citations.quote: God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father.

questions.prompt: Arius, the priest whose teaching Nicaea condemned, taught what about the Son?
choices: That the Son was a creature, brought into being by the Father and not eternally divine
That the Son and the Father are simply two names for the same single person
That Christ had no real human nature at all, only the appearance of one
That the Holy Spirit alone is fully divine, not the Son
questions.correctAnswer: That the Son was a creature, brought into being by the Father and not eternally divine
questions.explanation: Arius's teaching -- 'there was a time when the Son was not' -- denied the Son's full, eternal divinity, treating him instead as the highest of creatures. Nicaea's whole purpose was answering exactly this claim.
questions.hint: This is the specific claim Nicaea's own creed, confessing the Son 'begotten, not made,' was written to directly answer.

citations.quote: God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father.

questions.prompt: Nicaea's creed describes the Son as 'consubstantial,' or of the same ____, with the Father -- the Greek term is 'homoousios.'
questions.explanation: This single word became the whole council's decisive theological stake in the ground -- not merely similar to the Father, but truly, fully sharing the same divine reality.
questions.hint: The Greek word 'homoousios' literally means 'same' plus this word.

citations.quote: The Son of God is 'begotten, not made, of the same substance (homoousios) as the Father.'

questions.prompt: True or False: Nicaea met only a little more than a decade after Christianity had gained legal toleration in the Roman Empire.
questions.explanation: True. The Edict of Milan (313) had ended active persecution barely twelve years before Nicaea (325) -- this council meets almost immediately after Christians could gather this openly for the very first time in the Church's history.
questions.hint: Consider how recently Christians had gained the legal freedom to gather this openly at all.

citations.quote: God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father.

questions.prompt: Match each fact about Nicaea (325) to what it involves.

pairs.right: Taught the Son was a created being, not eternally divine
The Greek term for the Son's shared substance with the Father
The Edict of Milan, barely twelve years before this council met

questions.explanation: This council did not happen in a vacuum -- it meets almost immediately after Christians gained the legal freedom to assemble this openly, to answer a real, urgent theological crisis.
questions.hint: One row names the heresy's own teacher; one names the key term; one names attendance; one sets the political backdrop.

citations.quote: God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father.

questions.prompt: True or False: The Emperor Constantine convened the Council of Nicaea, but it was the assembled bishops who defined what the Church believed there.
questions.explanation: True, and the distinction is worth holding onto. An emperor could summon bishops and pay for their travel; he could not settle a doctrinal question. Confusing convening with defining is the seed of the popular claim that Constantine decided Christian doctrine.
questions.hint: Separate who called the meeting from who determined its content.

questions.prompt: What was Nicaea's real, lasting significance beyond simply condemning one man's teaching?
choices: It established the pattern every later council follows -- bishops gathering to define the faith against error
It had, in the end, no lasting significance of any kind beyond its own immediate fourth-century controversy
It permanently and completely ended all future theological controversy within the whole Church forever
It was formally reversed by the very next ecumenical council that happened to meet afterward
questions.correctAnswer: It established the pattern every later council follows -- bishops gathering to define the faith against error
questions.explanation: Every later council this topic will cover -- Constantinople, Ephesus, Chalcedon, and beyond -- follows the same basic shape Nicaea sets here: a real crisis, bishops gathered, a clear definition issued.
questions.hint: Consider what basic shape every later council in this topic will keep repeating.

citations.quote: God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father.

questions.prompt: True or False: Nicaea's own creed, as issued in 325, was already the complete Nicene Creed said at Mass today, with nothing added later.
questions.explanation: False. Nicaea's 325 creed confessed the Son's divinity but said comparatively little about the Holy Spirit -- the fuller creed said at Mass today was completed by a second council, which the next level in this topic covers.
questions.hint: Consider what this level's own creed said, or did not yet say, about the Holy Spirit.

citations.quote: God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father.

questions.prompt: Given that Nicaea's own creed left the Holy Spirit's divinity comparatively undeveloped, what does the next level in this topic turn to?
choices: Constantinople I (381), completing the creed on the Spirit's divinity, and Ephesus (431)
A complete and exhaustive repeat of this same level's material about Nicaea
A jump forward directly to the Council of Trent in the 16th century
A subject entirely unrelated to the Trinity or to Christ's own identity
questions.correctAnswer: Constantinople I (381), completing the creed on the Spirit's divinity, and Ephesus (431)
questions.explanation: The next level picks up exactly where Nicaea's own creed leaves off -- completing the Trinitarian confession, then moving to the next real crisis the Church faced fifty years later.
questions.hint: This is exactly what the next level in this topic covers.

citations.quote: And in the Spirit, the holy, the lordly and life-giving one, proceeding forth from the Father, co-worshipped and co-glorified with Father and Son, the one who spoke through the prophets.

questions.prompt: The First Council of Constantinople, held in 381, completed the creed begun at Nicaea by affirming the divinity of which Person of the Trinity?
choices: The Holy Spirit
The Son
The Father
It did not address the Trinity
questions.explanation: Constantinople I extended Nicaea's confession of the Son's divinity to the Holy Spirit, completing the Trinitarian faith expressed in the Nicene Creed still prayed at Mass today.
questions.hint: This is the fourth-century council that finished the Creed Nicaea started.

citations.quote: And in the Spirit, the holy, the lordly and life-giving one, proceeding forth from the Father, co-worshipped and co-glorified with Father and Son, the one who spoke through the prophets.

questions.prompt: The creed recited at Mass on Sundays is more precisely called the Nicene-____ Creed, because a second council completed what the first began.
questions.explanation: Nicaea in 325 settled the Son's divinity; Constantinople in 381 completed the confession of the Holy Spirit. The creed said at Mass is the product of both, which is why the double name is the accurate one.
questions.hint: The second council in the name is the one that met in 381.

questions.prompt: Which 431 council confessed the unity of Christ's person and gave Mary the title Theotokos, in opposition to the Nestorian heresy?
choices: Ephesus
Nicaea
Chalcedon
Constantinople
questions.explanation: The Third Ecumenical Council, held at Ephesus in 431, confessed that the Word united a truly human nature to himself in one person, honoring Mary as Theotokos, 'Mother of God.'
questions.hint: Held in the city where St. Paul spent nearly three years, and where tradition holds Mary later lived.

citations.quote: the holy virgin is the mother of God, not as though the nature of the Word had the origin of its being from the holy virgin
The Word, uniting to himself in his person the flesh animated by a rational soul, became man.

questions.prompt: True or False: Nestorius, the heresy Ephesus condemned, taught that Christ was effectively two separate persons, one divine and one human, loosely joined together.
questions.explanation: True. Nestorius's teaching divided Christ's unity so sharply that Mary, on his account, could be called mother of the human Jesus but not properly 'Mother of God' -- exactly the claim Ephesus rejected by insisting Christ is one single Person.
questions.hint: Consider why this heresy made Nestorius reluctant to call Mary 'Mother of God' at all.

citations.quote: the holy virgin is the mother of God, not as though the nature of the Word had the origin of its being from the holy virgin

questions.prompt: Why did Ephesus insist on calling Mary 'Theotokos' rather than settling for the softer title 'Christotokos' (Christ-bearer), which Nestorius preferred?
choices: Because the title is really a statement about Christ's own unity of person, not primarily an honor for Mary herself
Because the Council believed Mary was herself divine
Because the title was simply a matter of local Ephesian devotional custom with no doctrinal content
Because Nestorius himself had proposed the title first
questions.correctAnswer: Because the title is really a statement about Christ's own unity of person, not primarily an honor for Mary herself
questions.explanation: This is the whole doctrinal stake of the title: if Christ is one Person, truly God and truly man, then the one Mary bore is truly God -- 'Christotokos' alone would leave open exactly the division Nestorius taught.
questions.hint: Ask what the title actually claims about Christ, not only about Mary.

citations.quote: The Word, uniting to himself in his person the flesh animated by a rational soul, became man.

questions.prompt: Match each fact about Constantinople I (381) and Ephesus (431) to what it involves.

pairs.right: Completed the creed by confessing the Holy Spirit's divinity
Confessed Christ as one Person, giving Mary the title Theotokos
Taught Christ was, in effect, two loosely joined persons
A real doctrinal stake about Christ's unity, not just a title for Mary

questions.explanation: Together, these two councils, separated by fifty years, answer two different but related questions -- who the Holy Spirit is, and how fully one Christ can be both God and man.
questions.hint: Two rows concern Constantinople's own creed; two concern the specific dispute Ephesus resolved.

citations.quote: the holy virgin is the mother of God, not as though the nature of the Word had the origin of its being from the holy virgin

questions.prompt: True or False: Both Constantinople I and Ephesus follow the same basic pattern Nicaea already established -- a real doctrinal crisis met by bishops gathering to issue a clear definition.
questions.explanation: True. Neither council invents a new method -- both apply the exact pattern the previous level in this topic already introduced, confirming Nicaea's approach was the beginning of a lasting practice, not a one-time event.
questions.hint: Recall the pattern the previous level in this topic already established as Nicaea's real, lasting significance.

citations.quote: And in the Spirit, the holy, the lordly and life-giving one, proceeding forth from the Father, co-worshipped and co-glorified with Father and Son, the one who spoke through the prophets.

questions.prompt: What real question, left open by Ephesus's own confession that Christ is one Person, does the very next council in this topic have to address?
choices: Exactly how Christ's two natures, divine and human, relate to one another within that single Person
Whether the Holy Spirit is truly divine, a question already fully settled
Whether Mary should be honored at all, a question Ephesus had already resolved
No real question remained open after Ephesus
questions.correctAnswer: Exactly how Christ's two natures, divine and human, relate to one another within that single Person
questions.explanation: Ephesus confessed Christ's unity of Person; it did not fully spell out how his divine and human natures relate within that one Person -- a real, unfinished question the next level's council takes up directly.
questions.hint: Consider what Ephesus's own confession -- one Person -- leaves still unexplained about that Person's two natures.

citations.quote: the holy virgin is the mother of God, not as though the nature of the Word had the origin of its being from the holy virgin

questions.prompt: True or False: Ephesus's confession of Christ as one Person, by itself, already fully answered every later christological question the Church would ever face.
questions.explanation: False. A further error, teaching Christ had effectively only one nature rather than two, arises within a generation of Ephesus -- the exact crisis the next level's council, Chalcedon, is convened to answer.
questions.hint: Consider what new, different error arises within a generation after Ephesus's own council.

citations.quote: the holy virgin is the mother of God, not as though the nature of the Word had the origin of its being from the holy virgin

questions.prompt: Given the real question left open about Christ's two natures, what does the next level in this topic turn to?
choices: Chalcedon (451), which defines how Christ's two natures relate within his one Person
A complete repeat of this same level's material about Constantinople I and Ephesus
A jump forward directly to the Council of Trent in the 16th century
A subject entirely unrelated to Christ's own identity or nature
questions.correctAnswer: Chalcedon (451), which defines how Christ's two natures relate within his one Person
questions.explanation: The next level completes this topic's opening arc on Christ's own identity -- the fourth and final council in the sequence that began with Nicaea, twenty years after Ephesus.
questions.hint: This is exactly what the next level in this topic covers.

citations.quote: To be acknowledged in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation... concurring in one Person and one Subsistence.
